opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I came to this as a physicist, and early on, my picture of AI was the old-fashioned one: you'd sit down and try to write out the rules of intelligence by hand. Logic, symbols, if-this-then-that. And honestly that never really grabbed me, because it felt hopeless. Intelligence doesn't seem like something you can just enumerate.

What changed things for me was realizing that machine learning flips that around. You don't program the intelligence directly. You set up a very flexible system with an enormous number of parameters, you show it a ton of data, and you let the statistics do the work. The behavior emerges from the training process rather than being specified up front.

And to a physicist, that's an incredibly familiar story. It's basically statistical mechanics. You have a huge number of microscopic components, each one simple and individually kind of meaningless, and out of their collective interactions you get emergent, macroscopic behavior that you can actually describe with relatively simple effective laws. Nobody tracks every molecule of a gas to understand pressure and temperature.

So once I saw deep learning that way, AI stopped looking like this ad hoc engineering problem and started looking like a natural science. There might be principles here, things like scaling laws and effective theories, that let us understand why these systems work, not just that they work. That shift from "intelligence as a set of rules" to "intelligence as an emergent statistical phenomenon" is really what pulled me in.

r001.rationale: The response compares machine learning’s emergent behavior to statistical mechanics and says that analogy changed the speaker’s view of AI. It does not identify physics as a source of ideas for the statistical approach itself.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so my background is in theoretical physics, and I came into this with the physicist's instinct that if you want to understand a system, you write down the fundamental laws and derive everything from there. And I think for a long time that's also how I imagined intelligence would have to work. You'd figure out the rules of reasoning, the symbolic structure, and build it up from first principles.

What changed my view was realizing that machine learning basically inverted that. Nobody hand-designed the representations in these models. You set up a very simple objective, you throw an enormous amount of data at a very large, fairly generic architecture, and the interesting structure emerges statistically from the optimization process. The intelligence, to whatever extent it's there, isn't put in by hand. It comes out of the data.

And that was striking to me for two reasons. One is that it just worked, which honestly a lot of us wouldn't have predicted. The other is that it made the whole thing look a lot more like physics than like engineering. When you have a system with billions of parameters and you care about its collective behavior rather than any individual weight, that's exactly the regime where statistical mechanics lives. You stop asking what each piece is doing and start asking what the large-scale, emergent properties are, how they scale, what quantities control them.

So rather than thinking of AI as something you build by specifying rules, I started thinking of it as a natural phenomenon you can study. These models are objects with regularities, scaling laws, phase-transition-like behaviors, and you can actually do theory about them. That reframing is what pulled me in. It felt like a new branch of physics was opening up, and the system we were studying happened to be one we'd made ourselves.

r001.rationale: The response connects statistical mechanics to studying large machine-learning models, but it does not identify physics as a source of ideas for the statistical approach itself.

astra-6.text:
What changed my view was the idea that you didn’t have to explicitly program every aspect of intelligent behavior. You could specify a learning process, give it examples, and let it discover patterns that you might not know how to write down yourself.

That made the problem feel much more concrete to me. Instead of starting with, “What is intelligence, and how do we reproduce it?” you could ask, “What can this system learn from data? How well does it generalize to something it hasn’t seen? And how does that change as we give it more data or more capacity?” Those are questions you can test.

It didn’t resolve every question about intelligence. But it gave me a way to think about progress scientifically: build a model, measure what it does, and try to understand why it works.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes learning from examples and evaluating generalization, but does not identify physics as a source of ideas.

sol-6.1.text:
What changed my view was the idea that you didn’t have to explicitly program every rule for intelligent behavior. You could build a system that learned patterns from examples, and then ask whether those patterns helped it handle something it hadn’t seen before.

That made artificial intelligence feel like a concrete scientific problem. Instead of starting with a complete theory of how thinking works, you could choose a model, train it on data, measure its mistakes, and improve it. And the mistakes themselves became interesting: what had the system actually learned, and where did that learning break down?

It didn’t mean that learning patterns was the whole story of intelligence. But it gave us a powerful way to make progress without having to solve that whole story first.

r001.rationale: The response explains learning from examples and measuring model errors, but does not identify physics as a source of ideas for the statistical approach.
